questions.stem: What is a 「かたみちきっぷ」?
options: A return ticket
A reserved-seat ticket
A one-day pass
A one-way ticket
questions.explanation: 「かたみち」 means one way, so a 「かたみちきっぷ」 takes you to your destination only. A return ticket is an 「おうふくきっぷ」, which covers the trip there and back.

questions.stem: A station attendant tells you 「東京駅でやまのてせんに乗りかえてください。」 What should you do?
options: Stay on the Yamanote Line until Tokyo Station
Change to the Yamanote Line at Tokyo Station
Get off at Tokyo Station and walk from there
Buy a Yamanote Line ticket before you reach Tokyo
questions.explanation: 「乗りかえる」 means to change trains or transfer, and 「で」 marks Tokyo Station as the place where the change happens. Staying on the line until Tokyo would need 「まで」, not 「で」 with 「乗りかえる」.

questions.stem: You want a seat on a crowded shinkansen that is kept for you. Which do you ask for?
options: じゆうせき
ゆうせんせき
きんえんせき
していせき
questions.explanation: A 「していせき」 is a reserved seat: your ticket names the car and seat number. A 「じゆうせき」 is unreserved, so on a busy train you may have to stand, and a 「ゆうせんせき」 is a priority seat for people who need it more.

questions.stem: What is a 「ゆうせんせき」 on a Japanese train?
options: A fold-down seat used only when the train is full
A seat set aside for elderly, pregnant or disabled passengers
A seat that must be booked and paid for in advance
A seat in the first car, kept for women at peak hour
questions.explanation: 「ゆうせん」 means priority, and these seats near the doors are for older people, pregnant women, people with disabilities and those with small children. Booking a particular seat in advance is what a 「していせき」 is for.

questions.stem: What does the sign 「電車の中では、けいたいをマナーモードにしてください。」 ask passengers to do?
options: Turn their phones off before boarding
Keep their phones in their bags at all times
Make calls only in the space between cars
Set their phones to silent mode on the train
questions.explanation: 「マナーモード」 is the silent or vibrate setting on a phone, and 「〜にしてください」 asks you to switch it to that. The sign does not ask for phones to be turned off, which would be 「けいたいをけしてください」 or a similar request.

questions.stem: Which behaviour is generally seen as poor manners on a Japanese commuter train?
options: Queuing on the platform before boarding
Letting passengers off before getting on
Talking loudly on a mobile phone
Reading a book while standing
questions.explanation: Phone calls on trains are discouraged because they disturb the quiet that passengers expect. Queuing at the marked spots and letting people off first are the expected manners, not breaches of them.

questions.stem: What does the announcement 「つぎの電車は三番ホームから出ます。」 mean?
options: The next train has three carriages
The next train leaves from platform 3
The next train arrives at three o'clock
The next train stops at three stations
questions.explanation: 「三番ホーム」 is platform number 3, and 「から出ます」 means it departs from there. A time would use 「三時」, and a number of carriages would be counted, not given a platform number.

questions.stem: Your friend says 「しゅうでんは十一時半だから、十一時には店を出よう。」 Why does she want to leave at eleven?
options: Because the express train leaves at eleven
So they do not miss the last train of the night
So they can catch the first train in the morning
Because the shop closes at half past eleven
questions.explanation: 「しゅうでん」 is the last train of the day, here at 11.30, so leaving at eleven gives time to reach the station. The first train of the morning is 「しはつ」, and nothing in the sentence says when the shop closes.

questions.stem: What is an IC card such as Suica mainly used for in Japan?
options: Booking reserved seats on the shinkansen up to a month in advance
Getting a discount on hotel rooms for visitors from overseas
Proving your identity when you check in at a ryokan
Tapping on and off trains and buses, and paying in many shops
questions.explanation: Rechargeable IC cards are touched on the reader at the ticket gates, so you do not need to buy a ticket for each trip, and many convenience stores accept them as payment. Reserved seats are still bought as tickets or through the rail company.

questions.stem: 「この道をつきあたりまで行って、左にまがると、ゆうびんきょくがあります。」 How do you get to the post office?
options: Go to the end of this road and turn right
Go to the end of this road and turn left
Go straight past the end of the road on the left
Turn left at the first corner on this road
questions.explanation: 「つきあたり」 is the point where a road ends, often at a T-junction, and 「左にまがると」 means when you turn left. The post office appears after both steps, so turning at the first corner misses the 「つきあたりまで」 part.

questions.stem: Which question asks how long it takes to get to Kyoto by shinkansen?
options: 「京都までしんかんせんでどのぐらいかかりますか。」
「京都までしんかんせんでいくらかかりますか。」
「京都へしんかんせんで行ったことがありますか。」
「京都行きのしんかんせんは何時に出ますか。」
questions.explanation: 「どのぐらいかかりますか」 asks how long something takes. 「いくらかかりますか」 uses the same verb but asks how much it costs, which is the most tempting slip.

questions.stem: You ring a ryokan to book. Which sentence asks for a room for two people on 3 August?
options: 「八月三日に二人で行ったことがありますが、へやはどうですか。」
「八月二日に三人でとまりたいんですが、へやはありますか。」
「八月三日まで二人でとまっていますが、へやはどこですか。」
「八月三日に二人でとまりたいんですが、へやはありますか。」
questions.explanation: 「とまりたいんですが」 politely introduces what you want, and 「へやはありますか」 asks whether a room is free. 「八月二日に三人で」 swaps the numbers: the second of August for three people.

questions.stem: What does 「よやくをへんこうしたいんですが。」 mean?
options: I would like to change my booking.
I would like to cancel my booking.
I would like to confirm my booking.
I would like to make a booking.
questions.explanation: 「へんこう」 means a change, so the speaker wants to alter an existing booking. Cancelling is 「キャンセル」 or 「とりけし」, and making a new booking is simply 「よやくしたいんですが」.

questions.stem: At the hotel desk you hear 「チェックインは午後三時からでございます。」 What are you told?
options: Check-out is at 3 p.m.
Check-in takes about three hours
You can check in from 3 p.m.
You must check in before 3 p.m.
questions.explanation: 「午後三時から」 means from 3 p.m. onwards, and 「でございます」 is a very polite form of 「です」 used by hotel staff. A deadline would use 「までに」, not 「から」.

questions.stem: What does 「一泊朝食つき」 mean on a ryokan price list?
options: One night with all meals included
One night, with breakfast extra
One meal a day for each night
One night with breakfast included
questions.explanation: 「一泊」 is one night's stay, and 「〜つき」 means 'with' or 'included', so breakfast (「朝食」) comes with the room. A stay with dinner as well would be 「一泊二食つき」.

questions.stem: In a ryokan, what is the 「ゆかた」 left in your room for?
options: A heavy formal kimono for the dinner served in your room
A cotton sheet that covers the futon when it is laid out
A cloth for wiping your feet before you step on the tatami
A light cotton robe to wear around the inn and to the bath
questions.explanation: Ryokan provide a 「ゆかた」, a light cotton robe, which guests may wear in the corridors, at meals and on the way to the bath. It is casual wear, not the formal silk kimono worn for ceremonies.

questions.stem: When you put on a 「ゆかた」, how should the front panels be crossed?
options: Either way, as long as the belt is tied
Edge to edge, with no overlap at all
The left panel over the right one
The right panel over the left one
questions.explanation: A 「ゆかた」 or kimono is worn with the left side on top, so the right side goes on first, underneath. Right over left is used only when dressing the dead for a funeral, which is why getting it wrong is a well-known mistake.

questions.stem: What should you do before getting into the bath at an 「おんせん」?
options: Get in quickly and wash once you are in the water
Put on a swimsuit in the changing room first
Shower only after you have had your soak
Wash and rinse your body at the washing area first
questions.explanation: The bath water is shared and is for soaking, not washing, so you wash and rinse thoroughly at the taps first. Swimsuits are not normally worn in an 「おんせん」.

questions.stem: In an 「おんせん」, what should you do with your small towel?
options: Leave it floating in the water so that it does not get lost
Keep it out of the water, for example folded on your head
Wrap it around your waist while you sit in the water
Rinse it out in the bath water so that it stays clean
questions.explanation: Towels are kept out of the shared bath water because they would make it dirty, so people fold them on their heads or leave them at the edge. Wrapping it round your waist puts it in the water, which is the common mistake.

questions.stem: In a ryokan, what do you do before stepping onto the 「たたみ」 of a 「和室」?
options: Put on a pair of slippers
Put on your outdoor shoes
Wipe the floor with a towel
Take off your slippers
questions.explanation: Slippers are worn in corridors but taken off at the edge of a tatami room, which is walked on in socks or bare feet. Shoes are already left at the entrance.

questions.stem: In a Japanese home or ryokan, what are the slippers kept in the toilet for?
options: Wearing anywhere in the house after a bath
Taking home as a gift from your stay
Wearing outside in the garden or on the street
Wearing only in the toilet, then leaving them there
questions.explanation: Separate slippers are kept just inside the toilet; you change into them there and change back when you leave. Walking out into the rest of the house still wearing them is a classic visitor's mistake.

questions.stem: In a traditional ryokan room, where do guests usually sleep?
options: On cushions arranged around the low table
On a raised wooden platform by the window
On futon laid out on the tatami in the evening
On a western bed in a separate bedroom
questions.explanation: In a 「和室」 the same room is used for meals and sleeping: 「ふとん」 are taken out of the cupboard and spread on the tatami, often by staff, in the evening. Floor cushions are for sitting, not sleeping.

questions.stem: Handing a small gift to your host, which phrase is a traditional humble expression?
options: 「つまらないものですが、どうぞ。」
「とても高いものですから、どうぞ。」
「では、いただきます。」
「おまたせしました。どうぞ。」
questions.explanation: 「つまらないものですが」 literally calls the gift 'a trifling thing', which plays it down out of modesty; many people now say 「ほんの気もちですが」 instead. Pointing out that it was expensive does the opposite, and 「いただきます」 is said by the one receiving.

questions.stem: Your host says 「どうぞ、上がってください。」 at the door. What does she want you to do?
options: Come in, stepping up into the house
Go upstairs to your room straight away
Wait at the door for a moment
Put your bag up on the shelf
questions.explanation: Japanese homes have a step up from the 「げんかん」, so 「上がる」 means to come in. It does not mean going upstairs here: the host is inviting you inside.

questions.stem: At the end of a visit, as you leave your friend's home, which phrase fits?
options: 「おじゃましました。」
「おじゃまします。」
「ただいま。」
「いってきます。」
questions.explanation: 「おじゃましました」 ('I have disturbed you') is said when leaving someone's home, while 「おじゃまします」, in the present, is said when going in. 「ただいま」 and 「いってきます」 are said by people who live in the house.

questions.stem: After taking off your shoes in the 「げんかん」 of a Japanese home, what is the polite thing to do?
options: Leave them where they fell
Put them on the step inside
Turn them to face the door
Carry them in to your room
questions.explanation: Shoes are left in the lower part of the 「げんかん」, neatly placed facing the door so they are easy to step into when you leave. Putting them on the raised step brings outdoor dirt into the house.

questions.stem: Your host mother says 「えんりょしないで、たくさん食べてね。」 What does she mean?
options: You don't have to eat what you don't like
Don't hold back, eat as much as you like
Please don't eat too much tonight
Wait until everyone else has started eating
questions.explanation: 「えんりょしないで」 means 'without holding back', using the ない base + で, and 「たくさん 食べてね」 urges you to eat plenty. It is the opposite of asking you to eat less.

questions.stem: How are gifts and business cards usually handed over in Japan?
options: With the right hand only, held at arm's length
Placed on the table rather than handed over
With the left hand, keeping the right one free
With both hands, often with a slight bow
questions.explanation: Using both hands shows care and respect for the person and the object, and a small bow often goes with it. Passing something casually with one hand can seem offhand.

questions.stem: At the end of a meal, which sentence asks for the bill?
options: 「おかわり、おねがいします。」
「メニュー、おねがいします。」
「ちゅうもん、おねがいします。」
「おかいけい、おねがいします。」
questions.explanation: 「おかいけい」 is the bill or payment, so this asks to pay. 「おかわり」 asks for a second helping, which is the closest-sounding mistake.

questions.stem: What does 「べつべつにはらえますか。」 ask?
options: Can I pay later?
Can we pay together?
Can we pay separately?
Can I pay by card?
questions.explanation: 「べつべつに」 means separately, each person on their own, and 「はらえますか」 is the potential form, 'can we pay'. Paying together is 「いっしょに」.

questions.stem: In some ramen shops, what is a 「しょっけん」?
options: A menu board on the wall showing the dishes of the day
A meal ticket bought from a machine and handed to the staff
A paper bib handed out to keep the soup off your clothes
A card stamped each visit to earn a free bowl later
questions.explanation: In a 「しょっけん」 shop you choose and pay at a machine near the door, then hand the ticket over, so no money changes hands at the counter. A card stamped for rewards is a 「ポイントカード」.

questions.stem: The shop assistant asks 「ふくろはいりますか。」 What does she want to know?
options: Whether the item is a gift
Whether you need a bag
Whether you want a receipt
Whether you are paying by card
questions.explanation: 「ふくろ」 is a bag and 「いりますか」 asks whether you need it. Shops in Japan now charge for plastic bags, so staff ask before giving one.

questions.stem: In a clothes shop, which sentence asks to try something on?
options: 「これ、プレゼントにしてください。」
「これ、いくらになりますか。」
「これ、しちゃくしてもいいですか。」
「これ、ほかの色はありますか。」
questions.explanation: 「しちゃく」 means trying clothes on, and 「〜てもいいですか」 asks permission. 「ほかの色は ありますか」 asks about other colours, a related but different request.

questions.stem: Before a meal in a Japanese restaurant, what is an 「おしぼり」?
options: A small dish of pickles served free
A paper napkin to put on your lap
A pair of chopsticks in a paper case
A damp hand towel for wiping your hands
questions.explanation: An 「おしぼり」 is a hot or cold damp towel brought to the table for wiping your hands before eating. Chopsticks in a paper wrapper are 「わりばし」.

questions.stem: Public rubbish bins are hard to find in many Japanese streets. What do people usually do with their rubbish?
options: Leave it neatly on the footpath
Hand it to any shop they walk past
Put it in the nearest garden
Carry it with them and take it home
questions.explanation: People are expected to take their rubbish home, where it is sorted for collection. Leaving it on the street, even neatly, is seen as bad manners.

questions.stem: Besides buying food, what can you commonly do at a Japanese 「コンビニ」?
options: Pay bills and send parcels
Renew a passport or visa
Open a bank account
Book a medical appointment
questions.explanation: Japanese convenience stores handle bill payments, parcel delivery, ticket sales and photocopying, and many have cash machines. Passports and bank accounts are dealt with by government offices and banks.

questions.stem: A traveller wants to see many old temples and shrines in a former capital. Where should she go?
options: 京都
北海道
おきなわ
東京
questions.explanation: Kyoto was Japan's capital for over a thousand years, from 794, and is famous for its temples and shrines. Tokyo is the present capital, and Hokkaido and Okinawa are known for nature rather than old capitals.

questions.stem: 「北海道は冬に雪が多いので、スキーをする人に人気があります。」 Why is Hokkaido popular in winter?
options: It is warm, so people escape the cold there
It has many old temples to visit in winter
It holds winter festivals with fireworks
It gets a lot of snow, so skiers go there
questions.explanation: 「雪が多いので」 gives the reason, a lot of snow, and 「スキーをする人に人気があります」 says it is popular with skiers. The sentence says nothing about temples or fireworks.

questions.stem: 「おきなわは日本の南にある島々で、一年中あたたかいです。」 What does the sentence say?
options: Okinawa is one large island in the north of Japan, warm only in summer
Okinawa is a southern city in Japan that is cold for most of the year
Okinawa is a group of islands in the south, warm in winter only
Okinawa is a group of islands in the south of Japan, warm all year
questions.explanation: 「南にある島々」 means islands in the south (々 repeats 島), and 「一年中」 means all year round. The last distractor gets the place right but limits the warmth to winter.

questions.stem: A ryokan notice reads 「おふろは午後三時から夜十一時まで、朝は六時から九時までです。」 Can a guest take a bath at 10 p.m.?
options: No, because evening bathing ends at 6 p.m.
Yes, but only after 6 a.m. the next day
Yes, because the bath is open until 11 p.m.
No, because the bath closes at 9 p.m.
questions.explanation: The evening session runs from 3 p.m. to 11 p.m., so 10 p.m. falls inside it. The 9 o'clock closing applies to the morning session, 6 to 9 a.m., which is the detail a quick reader confuses.
